prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

About 25% of the Milky Way globular clusters (GCs) exhibit unusually extended color distribution of stars in the horizontal-branch (HB) phase. This phenomenon is now best understood as due to the presence of helium enhanced second generation subpopulations, which has raised a possibility that these peculiar GCs might have a unique origin. Here we show that these GCs with extended HB are clearly distinct from other normal GCs in kinematics and mass. The GCs with extended HB are more massive than normal GCs, and are dominated by random motion with no correlation between kinematics and metallicity. Surprisingly, however, when they are excluded, most normal GCs in the inner halo show clear signs of dissipational collapse that apparently led to the formation of the disk. Normal GCs in the outer halo share their kinematic properties with the extended HB GCs, which is consistent with the accretion origin. Our result further suggests heterogeneous origins of GCs, and we anticipate this to be a starting point for more detailed investigations of Milky Way formation, including early mergers, collapse, and later accretion.

outputs.L2: Roughly one quarter of the Milky Way’s globular clusters (GCs) contain stars in the horizontal-branch (HB) stage whose colors span an unusually wide range. The most widely accepted explanation for this feature is the existence of helium-rich second-generation stellar populations, suggesting that these atypical clusters may have formed through a distinctive process. About one quarter of the Milky Way’s globular clusters have unusually extended horizontal-branch color distributions. These extended horizontal branches are generally thought to be linked to the presence of helium-enhanced second-generation stars within the clusters. Such stellar populations can alter the colors and temperatures of horizontal-branch stars, producing the broad or extended distributions observed in these systems.

Globular clusters with extended horizontal branches appear to differ systematically from more typical, or “normal,” globular clusters. These differences are seen both in their kinematic behavior and in their masses. In general, extended horizontal-branch clusters are more massive than normal clusters, suggesting that they may have had deeper gravitational potential wells capable of retaining enriched material from earlier generations of stars. This retained material could then have contributed to the formation of helium-rich second-generation populations.

Kinematically, extended horizontal-branch globular clusters are dominated by random motions rather than ordered rotation. They also show no clear correlation between kinematics and metallicity. This distinguishes them from many normal globular clusters, particularly those in the inner halo, where the motions of clusters show evidence of a more organized formation history.

Most normal globular clusters located in the inner halo exhibit kinematic signatures consistent with dissipational collapse. In this scenario, gas in the early Galaxy lost energy, collapsed inward, and formed stars and clusters while contributing to the buildup of the Galactic disk. The properties of these inner-halo normal clusters therefore suggest that they may be closely connected to the early, dissipative formation of the Milky Way and may have played a role in the processes that led to disk formation.

By contrast, normal globular clusters in the outer halo have kinematic properties more similar to those of extended horizontal-branch clusters. Their motions are less ordered and more dominated by random components, which is consistent with an accretion origin. This suggests that many outer-halo normal clusters, like extended horizontal-branch clusters, may have been acquired from smaller satellite galaxies that merged with the Milky Way over time. Overall, the distinction between normal and extended horizontal-branch globular clusters provides important insight into the different formation pathways that contributed to the assembly of the Galactic halo.
outputs.L4:
Milky Way globular clusters show a wide variety of horizontal-branch morphologies, and a particularly interesting subgroup consists of clusters with extended horizontal branches. These extended horizontal branches are often interpreted as evidence for multiple stellar populations, including a helium-enhanced second generation of stars. To better understand the origin of these systems, globular clusters with extended horizontal branches can be compared with more “normal” globular clusters in terms of their kinematic properties, masses, metallicities, and spatial distribution within the Galactic halo.

Such comparisons show that extended-horizontal-branch clusters differ systematically from normal clusters. They are, on average, more massive, suggesting that only sufficiently massive clusters were able to retain or recycle enriched material and form helium-enhanced second-generation stars. Their motions also indicate that they are largely supported by random velocities rather than by ordered Galactic rotation. This means that they do not show the same strong connection to the rotating disk component of the Milky Way as some normal inner-halo clusters do.

By contrast, many normal globular clusters located in the inner halo exhibit kinematic signatures consistent with dissipational collapse. In this scenario, gas in the early Milky Way lost energy, collapsed toward the Galactic center, and contributed to the formation of the Galactic disk while also forming some globular clusters. These clusters therefore appear to preserve evidence of an early, relatively coherent phase of Galaxy formation connected with disk buildup.

The differences between extended-horizontal-branch clusters and normal clusters suggest that the Milky Way globular cluster system did not form through a single process. Instead, it likely has a heterogeneous origin. Some clusters may have formed during the early dissipational collapse of the proto-Galaxy, some may have been created or altered during mergers, and others may have been accreted from dwarf galaxies later incorporated into the Milky Way. Extended-horizontal-branch clusters, with their high masses, complex stellar populations, and random-dominated kinematics, may represent systems with particularly unusual or external origins, or clusters that experienced more complex internal chemical evolution than typical globular clusters. Overall, the properties of these clusters provide important clues to the assembly history of the Milky Way halo and the diverse pathways through which globular clusters formed.

The Milky Way is the galaxy that contains our Solar System. It is a vast spiral galaxy made up of billions of stars, planets, clouds of gas, dust, and dark matter. From Earth, the Milky Way appears as a faint, glowing band across the night sky, especially visible in dark areas away from city lights.

Our Sun is just one of the many stars in the Milky Way. It is located in one of the galaxy’s spiral arms, called the Orion Arm. The center of the Milky Way lies about 26,000 light-years away from Earth and contains a supermassive black hole known as Sagittarius A*.

The Milky Way is enormous, stretching about 100,000 light-years across. It rotates slowly, and our Solar System takes roughly 225 to 250 million years to complete one orbit around the galaxy’s center. Scientists study the Milky Way to learn more about how galaxies form, how stars are born, and what the universe is made of.

The Milky Way is only one galaxy among billions in the universe, but it is special to us because it is our cosmic home.

counterfactuals.output: We investigate Milky Way globular clusters hosting extended horizontal branches (EHBs) as tracers of complex stellar populations and early Galactic assembly. Their hot horizontal-branch morphologies are consistent with substantial helium enhancement in second-generation stars, likely produced through self-enrichment in initially massive cluster systems. Compared with clusters lacking EHBs, these objects are typically more massive and often exhibit distinctive internal and orbital kinematics, including evidence for rotation, anisotropy, or accretion-linked trajectories. These properties suggest that EHB clusters retained processed material more efficiently and may represent the surviving nuclei or remnants of unusually massive star-forming environments. The association between helium-rich populations, large present-day masses, and non-standard kinematics supports a scenario in which at least some EHB globular clusters formed in dwarf-galaxy-like systems later accreted by the Milky Way. EHB clusters therefore provide a key fossil record of multiple-population formation, cluster mass loss, and the hierarchical build-up of the Galactic halo.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main findings of a study comparing extended-HB globular clusters with normal Galactic globular clusters in terms of mass, metallicity correlations, inner/outer halo kinematics, and possible origins.
counterfactuals.output:
The study found that globular clusters with **extended horizontal branches (EHBs)** are not simply the tail end of the normal Galactic globular-cluster population. They appear to be a distinct subset in several respects:

- **Mass / luminosity**
  - EHB clusters are, on average, **more massive and more luminous** than normal Galactic globular clusters.
  - Many of them rank among the most massive clusters in the Milky Way system.
  - This supports the idea that they were massive enough to retain enriched gas and form multiple stellar populations, including helium-enhanced stars that can populate very hot HB extensions.

- **Metallicity and HB morphology**
  - Normal globular clusters show the expected broad connection between **metallicity and horizontal-branch morphology**: metal-poor clusters tend to have bluer HBs.
  - EHB clusters do not follow this relation in a simple way. Their very extended blue HBs occur over a range of metallicities and require an additional “second parameter,” likely related to cluster mass, helium enrichment, age, or internal chemical complexity.
  - The presence of EHBs is therefore not explained by metallicity alone.

- **Inner- and outer-halo kinematics**
  - When divided into inner- and outer-halo samples, EHB clusters show kinematic behavior that differs from normal clusters.
  - Normal inner-halo clusters tend to show more coherent Galactic rotation, consistent with an in-situ or early-collapsed halo population.
  - EHB clusters, especially those in the outer halo, have more halo-like or accretion-like orbital properties, with higher velocity dispersion and less organized rotation.
  - Their kinematics suggest that many EHB clusters may not have formed in the same way as the ordinary inner-halo globular clusters.

- **Possible origins**
  - The study argues that EHB clusters may be linked to **accreted dwarf-galaxy systems** or to the dense nuclei of former dwarf galaxies.
  - Their high masses, complex stellar populations, unusual HB morphologies, and distinct orbital properties are consistent with an origin in larger parent systems that were later disrupted by the Milky Way.
  - Some massive EHB clusters, such as ω Centauri or M54-like objects, are often interpreted as possible stripped dwarf-galaxy nuclei.

Overall, the main conclusion is that **extended-HB globular clusters are generally more massive, chemically and dynamically unusual, and possibly of external or dwarf-galaxy origin**, rather than being ordinary Galactic globular clusters whose HBs are determined only by metallicity.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an academic abstract for a research article arguing that extended horizontal branch globular clusters are kinematically distinct and may have an accretion origin, while normal inner-halo clusters trace dissipational collapse.
counterfactuals.output:
This study investigates the relationship between horizontal-branch morphology and Galactic globular-cluster kinematics in order to assess the origin of extended horizontal branch (EHB) clusters in the Milky Way halo. Using published structural parameters, metallicities, horizontal-branch classifications, and full space motions for a representative sample of Galactic globular clusters, we compare the orbital properties of EHB systems with those of clusters exhibiting normal horizontal branches, with particular emphasis on inner-halo populations. The analysis shows that EHB clusters occupy a kinematically distinct regime: relative to normal inner-halo clusters, they exhibit larger orbital energies, more eccentric orbits, broader angular-momentum distributions, and a reduced tendency to participate in coherent prograde rotation. Several EHB clusters are also associated with large apogalactic distances and orbital properties more typical of accreted halo debris than of a centrally concentrated, dissipatively formed population.

By contrast, normal inner-halo clusters display kinematic signatures consistent with formation during an early dissipational collapse of the proto-Galaxy, including stronger spatial concentration, lower orbital energies, and more coherent rotational behavior. These differences persist at fixed metallicity, indicating that horizontal-branch morphology is not solely a consequence of chemical abundance but is linked to differences in formation environment and subsequent dynamical history. We argue that EHB clusters are preferentially associated with systems accreted from dwarf-galaxy progenitors, where extended star-formation histories, helium enrichment, or multiple stellar populations could have contributed to the development of extreme horizontal-branch morphologies. The results support a dual-origin picture for the Galactic globular-cluster system, in which normal inner-halo clusters preserve the kinematic imprint of dissipational collapse, whereas EHB clusters represent, at least in part, an accreted component of the stellar halo.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: In the style of an astronomy journal abstract, describe evidence that extended horizontal branch globular clusters are massive, randomly moving systems linked to accretion, and contrast them with normal inner-halo clusters associated with disk-forming collapse.
counterfactuals.output:
We present evidence that Galactic globular clusters with extended horizontal branches (EHBs) constitute a distinct dynamical and evolutionary subsystem of the Milky Way halo.  Relative to normal inner-halo clusters of comparable metallicity, EHB clusters are systematically more luminous and massive, indicating either unusually efficient early star formation or survival as the dense remnants of more massive progenitors.  Their Galactic kinematics are dominated by large, apparently random motions: they show little net rotation, high orbital energy, and a broad distribution of eccentricities and inclinations.  These properties are consistent with an accreted population assembled from disrupted dwarf galaxies, in which EHB clusters may represent former nuclear or massive cluster systems capable of retaining enriched material and producing multiple stellar populations, including helium-enhanced stars responsible for the extended blue horizontal branch morphology.

This behavior contrasts with that of normal inner-halo globular clusters, which are less massive on average and exhibit kinematics more closely coupled to the early dissipative formation of the Galaxy.  The normal inner-halo population shows a more centrally concentrated spatial distribution, a greater degree of rotational coherence, and properties compatible with formation during the rapid collapse that also contributed to the proto-disk.  In this picture, EHB clusters trace a later, stochastic accretion history of the Galactic halo, whereas normal inner-halo clusters preserve the signature of an earlier, more ordered disk-forming collapse.  The horizontal-branch morphology, cluster mass scale, and orbital characteristics therefore jointly support a dual-origin interpretation of the Milky Way globular cluster system.
